🗓️14-Week Study Plan — recommended path through this index

▶

Designed for a ~10 hr/week pace. Adjust based on your prior experience. The order is foundation-first: each later pattern builds on something earlier.

Week
1–2
Foundation: Arrays & Linear Patterns
🎯 Solve 30 problems
Build intuition for index manipulation, sliding windows, and prefix-sum tricks. These appear in 30% of interviews.
P1: Two Pointer Patterns P2: Array/Matrix Manipulation Patterns P5: Sliding Window Patterns P17: Prefix Sum & Difference Array Patterns
Week
3–4
Linear Data Structures
🎯 Solve 25 problems
Linked lists (reversal, fast/slow), stack patterns (monotonic, parens), heaps (top K, two heaps for median).
P3: Linked List Manipulation Patterns P6: Stack Patterns P7: Heap (Priority Queue) Patterns
Week
5
Searching & Hashing
🎯 Solve 20 problems
Binary search templates (including binary search on answer), hashmap design (LRU/LFU), and bit tricks.
P8: Binary Search Patterns P18: Hash Map & Cache Design Patterns P14: Bit Manipulation Patterns
Week
6–7
Trees
🎯 Solve 25 problems
DFS/BFS traversals, LCA, serialization. Tree DP (diameter, max path sum) is the highest-leverage subset.
P4: Tree Traversal Patterns (DFS & BFS) P22: Tree Dynamic Programming Patterns
Week
8–10
Graphs
🎯 Solve 35 problems
BFS/DFS on grids, topological sort, Union-Find, Dijkstra. Advanced graph (Tarjan, Bellman-Ford) for senior interviews.
P9: Graph Traversal Patterns (DFS & BFS) P25: Multi-Source BFS Patterns P24: Advanced Graph Algorithm Patterns
Week
11–12
Dynamic Programming
🎯 Solve 30 problems
1D Kadane/Knapsack first, then 2D LCS/Edit Distance, then advanced (bitmask, interval). The hardest area for most candidates.
P12: Dynamic Programming (DP) Patterns P23: Advanced Dynamic Programming Patterns
Week
13
Backtracking & Greedy
🎯 Solve 15 problems
Subsets/permutations template, N-Queens, interval scheduling. Greedy proofs are often the trickiest part.
P10: Greedy Patterns P11: Backtracking Patterns
Week
14
Advanced & Niche
🎯 Solve 15 problems (pick highest-relevance to your target companies)
Segment/Fenwick trees, Trie, Line Sweep, Manacher, Z-algorithm. Only needed for senior/competitive roles or specific company prep.
P16: Segment Tree & Fenwick Tree Patterns P20: Trie / Prefix Tree Patterns P21: Intervals & Line Sweep Patterns P27: Sorting Algorithms & Selection Patterns P28: Randomized Algorithm Patterns P29: Advanced String Algorithm Patterns
Week
15+
Mock Interviews & Spaced Repetition
🎯 2–3 mocks/week, re-solve weak problems
Solving alone ≠ interviewing well. Use Pramp or interviewing.io for live practice. Use the Bookmark feature to flag re-review candidates.

Practice System: Drills & Meta-Skills

The audit flagged these practice habits as missing. Use them as your weekly operating system.

Weekly drills

Practice operating system

  • Pattern recognition drill: read 5 unseen problem statements, name the pattern in under 60 seconds each, no solving.
  • Complexity trade-off drill: for each solved problem, state an alternative approach and why its time/space trade is worse.
  • Edge-case checklist: empty input, single element, duplicates, negatives, overflow, sorted/reverse-sorted, max constraints.
  • Mock communication drill: solve one problem out loud in 25 minutes — restate, plan, code, test, complexity.
  • Re-solve queue: every bookmarked ★ problem returns in 7 days; solved-with-help returns in 3.

Two Pointer Patterns

7 subpatterns · 37 problems
0 / 37
Use two indices to traverse a structure in coordinated ways — converge, chase, or scan from both ends.
When to use. Sorted arrays, palindrome checks, in-place mutation, linked-list cycle/middle detection, and any O(n²) brute force that can collapse to O(n).
Key idea. Maintain two pointers with an invariant (sum, distance, parity) and advance them based on a comparison; eliminate one direction of search per step.
Complexity. Typically O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
💻 Code Template — Two Pointers — converging ▶ 
def two_pointers(arr, target):
    left, right = 0, len(arr) - 1
    while left < right:
        s = arr[left] + arr[right]
        if s == target:
            return [left, right]
        elif s < target:
            left += 1
        else:
            right -= 1
    return [-1, -1]

# Fast & slow (Floyd's cycle):
def has_cycle(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
        if slow == fast:
            return True
    return False

Array/Matrix Manipulation Patterns

10 subpatterns · 24 problems
0 / 24
Manipulate 1D arrays and 2D matrices in place — rotations, traversals, marking, and prefix transforms.
When to use. When you must avoid extra O(n) space, when matrix geometry matters (rotation, spiral, diagonal), or when one pass with bookkeeping replaces multiple passes.
Key idea. Use indices, signs, or sentinel values inside the existing array as bookkeeping; transform geometry by swapping layers/rows/columns.
Complexity. O(n) or O(rows×cols) time, O(1) extra space when fully in-place.

Linked List Manipulation Patterns

5 subpatterns · 22 problems
0 / 22
Surgical pointer manipulation on singly/doubly linked lists — reverse, merge, partition, and detect.
When to use. Whenever the input is a linked list and you need O(1) extra space, or when the problem implies in-place restructuring.
Key idea. Use a dummy head node and 2–3 pointers (prev, curr, next) to rewire links without losing references.
Complexity. O(n) time, O(1) extra space for most variants.

Tree Traversal Patterns (DFS & BFS)

6 subpatterns · 54 problems
0 / 54
Recursive and iterative tree traversals — BFS for level-by-level, DFS preorder/inorder/postorder for structure.
When to use. Binary trees, BSTs, n-ary trees, level-order problems, ancestor problems, path/sum problems, and serialization.
Key idea. Pick the traversal that exposes the property you need — inorder for sorted BST, postorder for child-then-self computation, BFS for shortest depth.
Complexity. O(n) time, O(h) space (h = height) for recursion stack, O(width) for BFS.

Pattern 5 of 29

Sliding Window Patterns

4 subpatterns · 33 problems
0 / 33
Maintain a window over a sequence that grows/shrinks based on a condition — fixed-size or variable.
When to use. Contiguous subarrays/substrings with sum, length, distinct-count, or frequency constraints.
Key idea. Two pointers define the window; expand the right, contract the left when the condition is violated, track answer on each valid window.
Complexity. O(n) amortized — each element enters and exits the window once.
💻 Code Template — Variable Sliding Window ▶ 
def longest_subarray(s, k):
    left = 0
    result = 0
    counts = {}  # window state
    for right in range(len(s)):
        counts[s[right]] = counts.get(s[right], 0) + 1
        # shrink while invalid
        while len(counts) > k:
            counts[s[left]] -= 1
            if counts[s[left]] == 0:
                del counts[s[left]]
            left += 1
        result = max(result, right - left + 1)
    return result

Pattern 6 of 29

Stack Patterns

6 subpatterns · 32 problems
0 / 32
LIFO data structure for matching, expression evaluation, and monotonic-property problems.
When to use. Balanced brackets, next-greater/next-smaller, expression parsing, simulation with backtracking, histogram problems.
Key idea. Push when a condition is open or unresolved; pop when it's matched/closed. A monotonic stack maintains sorted order to answer range queries.
Complexity. O(n) amortized; each element pushed/popped at most once.
💻 Code Template — Monotonic Stack ▶ 
def next_greater(arr):
    result = [-1] * len(arr)
    stack = []  # indices, values decreasing
    for i, v in enumerate(arr):
        while stack and arr[stack[-1]] < v:
            idx = stack.pop()
            result[idx] = v
        stack.append(i)
    return result

Pattern 7 of 29

Heap (Priority Queue) Patterns

4 subpatterns · 30 problems
0 / 30
Priority queue for streaming top-K, median, k-way merge, and scheduling problems.
When to use. When you need the smallest/largest k elements, repeatedly extract min/max, or schedule by cost/deadline/frequency.
Key idea. Maintain a heap of size k (for top-k) or two heaps balanced around the median; push/pop are O(log n).
Complexity. O(n log k) for top-k, O(log n) per insert/extract.
💻 Code Template — Top K with Heap ▶ 
import heapq
def top_k_frequent(nums, k):
    counts = {}
    for n in nums:
        counts[n] = counts.get(n, 0) + 1
    # Min-heap of size K
    heap = []
    for num, freq in counts.items():
        heapq.heappush(heap, (freq, num))
        if len(heap) > k:
            heapq.heappop(heap)
    return [num for freq, num in heap]

VIII
Pattern 8 of 29

Binary Search Patterns

5 subpatterns · 29 problems
0 / 29
Logarithmic search on a monotonic structure — sorted arrays, rotated arrays, or 'monotonic predicate on the answer'.
When to use. Sorted/rotated input, or when you can frame the answer as 'find the smallest/largest value for which a check function flips from false to true.'
Key idea. Maintain [lo, hi] with an invariant; halve the range each step. The hardest variant is binary search on the answer (parametric search).
Complexity. O(log n) for direct search, O(n log answer-range) for binary search on the answer.
💻 Code Template — Binary Search — lower_bound template ▶ 
def lower_bound(arr, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(arr)  # [lo, hi)
    while lo < hi:
        mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2
        if arr[mid] < target:
            lo = mid + 1
        else:
            hi = mid
    return lo  # first index where arr[i] >= target

# Binary search on answer:
def min_value_satisfying(lo, hi, ok):
    while lo < hi:
        mid = lo + (hi - lo) // 2
        if ok(mid):
            hi = mid
        else:
            lo = mid + 1
    return lo

Pattern 9 of 29

Graph Traversal Patterns (DFS & BFS)

11 subpatterns · 69 problems
0 / 65
Graph traversal foundations — DFS/BFS for components, cycles, topological order, shortest paths, and connectivity.
When to use. Any problem framed on nodes and edges: islands, courses, network flow, dependencies, coloring, MST.
Key idea. Choose the right traversal: DFS for path/cycle/topological, BFS for unweighted shortest path, Dijkstra for weighted, Union-Find for connectivity queries.
Complexity. O(V+E) for DFS/BFS, O((V+E) log V) for Dijkstra, O(E α(V)) for Union-Find.
💻 Code Template — BFS, DFS, Dijkstra, Union-Find ▶ 
# BFS
from collections import deque
def bfs(start, graph):
    visited = {start}
    q = deque([start])
    while q:
        node = q.popleft()
        for nb in graph[node]:
            if nb not in visited:
                visited.add(nb)
                q.append(nb)

# Dijkstra with min-heap
import heapq
def dijkstra(start, graph, n):
    dist = [float('inf')] * n
    dist[start] = 0
    pq = [(0, start)]
    while pq:
        d, u = heapq.heappop(pq)
        if d > dist[u]: continue
        for v, w in graph[u]:
            if dist[u] + w < dist[v]:
                dist[v] = dist[u] + w
                heapq.heappush(pq, (dist[v], v))
    return dist

# Union-Find with path compression + union by rank
class DSU:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.parent = list(range(n))
        self.rank = [0] * n
    def find(self, x):
        while self.parent[x] != x:
            self.parent[x] = self.parent[self.parent[x]]
            x = self.parent[x]
        return x
    def union(self, x, y):
        px, py = self.find(x), self.find(y)
        if px == py: return False
        if self.rank[px] < self.rank[py]: px, py = py, px
        self.parent[py] = px
        if self.rank[px] == self.rank[py]: self.rank[px] += 1
        return True

Greedy Patterns

7 subpatterns · 25 problems
0 / 25
Make the locally optimal choice and prove it leads to a global optimum — often after sorting.
When to use. Interval scheduling, jump-reachability, partition-labels, frequency-based scheduling, exchange-argument problems.
Key idea. Sort by the right key (start, end, deadline, ratio) and process greedily; sometimes use a heap to track 'best available' option.
Complexity. Typically O(n log n) for the sort, then O(n) for the sweep.

Pattern 11 of 29

Backtracking Patterns

7 subpatterns · 27 problems
0 / 27
Systematic exploration of decision trees — choose, recurse, un-choose — with pruning.
When to use. Subsets, permutations, combinations, palindrome partitions, constraint satisfaction (N-Queens, Sudoku), path search in grids.
Key idea. Maintain a partial solution; at each step, try each valid choice, recurse, then undo. Prune branches that can't lead to a valid answer.
Complexity. Exponential in the worst case — O(2ⁿ), O(n!), or similar; pruning is critical.
💻 Code Template — Backtracking — subsets / permutations / N-Queens ▶ 
def subsets(nums):
    result = []
    path = []
    def backtrack(start):
        result.append(path[:])
        for i in range(start, len(nums)):
            path.append(nums[i])
            backtrack(i + 1)
            path.pop()
    backtrack(0)
    return result

def permutations(nums):
    result = []
    used = [False] * len(nums)
    path = []
    def backtrack():
        if len(path) == len(nums):
            result.append(path[:])
            return
        for i in range(len(nums)):
            if used[i]: continue
            used[i] = True
            path.append(nums[i])
            backtrack()
            path.pop()
            used[i] = False
    backtrack()
    return result

XII
Pattern 12 of 29

Dynamic Programming (DP) Patterns

12 subpatterns · 50 problems
0 / 50
Memoize overlapping subproblems and build optimal solutions from smaller ones.
When to use. Optimal substructure + overlapping subproblems: knapsack, edit distance, longest common subsequence, paths in a grid, palindrome problems.
Key idea. Define state precisely, write a recurrence, decide top-down (memoization) or bottom-up (tabulation), then optimize space when possible.
Complexity. Polynomial — states × transitions; classic DPs are O(n²) or O(n·m).
💻 Code Template — DP — top-down memo + bottom-up tabulation ▶ 
# Top-down with memo
from functools import lru_cache
def coin_change(coins, amount):
    @lru_cache(None)
    def dp(remain):
        if remain == 0: return 0
        if remain < 0: return float('inf')
        return min((dp(remain - c) + 1 for c in coins), default=float('inf'))
    result = dp(amount)
    return result if result != float('inf') else -1

# Bottom-up
def coin_change_bu(coins, amount):
    dp = [float('inf')] * (amount + 1)
    dp[0] = 0
    for i in range(1, amount + 1):
        for c in coins:
            if i - c >= 0:
                dp[i] = min(dp[i], dp[i - c] + 1)
    return dp[amount] if dp[amount] != float('inf') else -1

# 0/1 Knapsack template
def knapsack(weights, values, W):
    n = len(weights)
    dp = [0] * (W + 1)
    for i in range(n):
        for w in range(W, weights[i] - 1, -1):  # iterate right to left
            dp[w] = max(dp[w], dp[w - weights[i]] + values[i])
    return dp[W]

String Manipulation Patterns

7 subpatterns · 23 problems
0 / 23
Character-level algorithms — palindromes, anagrams, parsing, and pattern matching.
When to use. String comparison, frequency counting, integer/string conversion, substring search with linear-time guarantees.
Key idea. Use frequency arrays for anagrams, two pointers for palindromes, hashing for fast comparison, and KMP/Rabin-Karp for substring search.
Complexity. O(n) for most one-pass problems, O(n+m) for KMP, O(n) average for Rabin-Karp.

Bit Manipulation Patterns

4 subpatterns · 16 problems
0 / 16
Use binary representation as a data structure — XOR for cancellation, AND/OR for masks, shifts for power-of-two.
When to use. Finding singletons in pairs, counting set bits, subset enumeration via bitmask, modular arithmetic with bits.
Key idea. XOR is its own inverse (a^a=0), AND with (n-1) clears the lowest set bit, shifts multiply/divide by 2.
Complexity. Most operations are O(1) per bit, O(log n) per number.

XVI
Pattern 16 of 29

Segment Tree & Fenwick Tree Patterns

2 subpatterns · 12 problems
0 / 11
Tree-based range data structures — segment tree for arbitrary range queries, Fenwick (BIT) for prefix sums.
When to use. Range sum/min/max with point or range updates, inversion counting, online interval problems, coordinate compression.
Key idea. Segment tree is more flexible (lazy propagation for range updates); Fenwick is simpler and faster for prefix-sum style queries.
Complexity. O(n) build, O(log n) per query/update.
💻 Code Template — Iterative Segment Tree (sum) ▶ 
class SegTree:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.n = n
        self.t = [0] * (2 * n)
    def build(self, arr):
        for i, v in enumerate(arr):
            self.t[self.n + i] = v
        for i in range(self.n - 1, 0, -1):
            self.t[i] = self.t[2*i] + self.t[2*i + 1]
    def update(self, i, v):
        i += self.n
        self.t[i] = v
        while i > 1:
            i //= 2
            self.t[i] = self.t[2*i] + self.t[2*i + 1]
    def query(self, l, r):  # [l, r)
        l += self.n; r += self.n
        res = 0
        while l < r:
            if l & 1: res += self.t[l]; l += 1
            if r & 1: r -= 1; res += self.t[r]
            l //= 2; r //= 2
        return res

XVII
Pattern 17 of 29

Prefix Sum & Difference Array Patterns

4 subpatterns · 13 problems
0 / 13
Precompute cumulative sums for O(1) range queries; combine with hashmap for 'subarray equals target' even with negatives.
When to use. Subarray sum problems where sliding window fails (e.g., when negatives are allowed), range sum queries, range updates via difference array.
Key idea. prefix[i] = a[0]+…+a[i-1]; range sum = prefix[r+1]-prefix[l]. With hashmap, count subarrays whose prefix difference equals k.
Complexity. O(n) build, O(1) per range query; difference array gives O(1) range updates.
💻 Code Template — Prefix Sum + HashMap ▶ 
def subarray_sum_equals_k(nums, k):
    count = 0
    prefix = 0
    seen = {0: 1}  # prefix sum -> count
    for n in nums:
        prefix += n
        count += seen.get(prefix - k, 0)
        seen[prefix] = seen.get(prefix, 0) + 1
    return count

Pattern 20 of 29

Trie / Prefix Tree Patterns

5 subpatterns · 17 problems
0 / 17
A 26-ary (or 2-ary for XOR) tree where each path from root spells a string prefix.
When to use. Prefix lookup, autocomplete, word search in grids, replace-words, palindrome pairs, maximum-XOR-pair queries.
Key idea. Insert/search are O(L) where L is word length; combine with DFS/backtracking when searching a grid for many words at once.
Complexity. O(sum of word lengths) to build, O(L) per query.
💻 Code Template — Trie — insert / search / startsWith ▶ 
class TrieNode:
    def __init__(self):
        self.children = {}
        self.is_end = False

class Trie:
    def __init__(self):
        self.root = TrieNode()
    def insert(self, word):
        node = self.root
        for c in word:
            if c not in node.children:
                node.children[c] = TrieNode()
            node = node.children[c]
        node.is_end = True
    def search(self, word):
        node = self._traverse(word)
        return node is not None and node.is_end
    def starts_with(self, prefix):
        return self._traverse(prefix) is not None
    def _traverse(self, s):
        node = self.root
        for c in s:
            if c not in node.children: return None
            node = node.children[c]
        return node

Post-order DP on trees — each subtree returns one or more values used by its parent.
When to use. House Robber on a tree, diameter, max path sum, longest univalue path, max-sum BST.
Key idea. Recurse to children first; combine their return values (often a tuple like (include, exclude) or (max_path_ending_here, best_seen)) to compute the parent's answer.
Complexity. O(n) — each node is visited once.

Pattern 23 of 29

Advanced Dynamic Programming Patterns

5 subpatterns · 30 problems
0 / 30
DP where state encodes a subset (bitmask), a digit position (digit DP), or a finite mode (state machine).
When to use. Small-n exponential problems (n ≤ 20 for bitmask), counting integers ≤ N with digit constraints, stock problems with cooldown/fee.
Key idea. Bitmask DP: state = (mask, …); iterate over submasks or transitions. Digit DP: state = (position, tight, leading_zero, …). State machine: track which 'mode' you're in (holding, sold, cooldown).
Complexity. Bitmask: O(2ⁿ · n). Digit: O(digits · states · 10). State machine: O(n · states).

Pattern 24 of 29

Advanced Graph Algorithm Patterns

9 subpatterns · 27 problems
0 / 27
Algorithms beyond basic BFS/DFS — bridges, all-pairs, Eulerian paths, A*-style heuristics, 0-1 BFS.
When to use. Critical edges, all-pairs shortest path on small graphs, itinerary reconstruction, weighted-grid shortest paths, multi-state BFS.
Key idea. Tarjan for bridges/SCC, Floyd-Warshall for all-pairs (O(V³)), Hierholzer for Eulerian, 0-1 BFS for graphs with edge weights ∈ {0,1}, bidirectional BFS to halve depth.
Complexity. Tarjan O(V+E), Floyd-Warshall O(V³), Bellman-Ford O(V·E), 0-1 BFS O(V+E).

Pattern 25 of 29

Multi-Source BFS Patterns

1 subpatterns · 6 problems
0 / 6
Seed the BFS queue with ALL starting cells at distance 0 and expand simultaneously.
When to use. Multi-origin shortest-distance problems on grids: rotting fruit, walls and gates, distance to nearest 1, fire spread.
Key idea. Push every source into the queue with distance 0 in the same pass; the BFS naturally computes the minimum distance from any source.
Complexity. O(rows × cols) — every cell is visited once.

Iterator & Data-Stream Design Patterns

6 subpatterns · 13 problems
0 / 13
Lazy iteration over nested/structured data, plus streaming statistics on infinite input.
When to use. BST iterator, peeking iterator, zigzag iterator, nested list flattening, moving averages, streaming median.
Key idea. Defer work until next() is called; keep just enough state (stack of partial results, two heaps, deque) to answer the next query in O(1) or O(log n).
Complexity. Typically O(1) amortized per next()/hasNext().

Pattern 27 of 29

Sorting Algorithms & Selection Patterns

4 subpatterns · 8 problems
0 / 8
Use a sort (or partial sort) as the core technique — Quickselect, merge-sort applications, bucket/counting/radix sort.
When to use. Kth-element queries (Quickselect O(n) avg), inversion counting (merge sort), bounded-range counting (bucket/radix).
Key idea. Quickselect partitions around a pivot like Quicksort but recurses into one side; merge sort can count inversions during the merge step.
Complexity. Quickselect O(n) avg / O(n²) worst; merge-sort apps O(n log n); bucket/radix O(n + k).

Pattern 28 of 29

Randomized Algorithm Patterns

4 subpatterns · 6 problems
0 / 6
Uniform/weighted random selection in constant space, or sampling from streams of unknown length.
When to use. Pick random element from a stream/linked list, weighted random by frequency, random with blacklist, Fisher–Yates shuffle.
Key idea. Reservoir sampling keeps one or k samples and replaces with probability k/i at step i; weighted random uses prefix sums + binary search.
Complexity. O(n) one-pass for reservoir; O(log n) per query for weighted (after O(n) precomputation).

Pattern 29 of 29

Advanced String Algorithm Patterns

3 subpatterns · 7 problems
0 / 7
Linear-time string matching and palindrome structure beyond KMP/Rabin-Karp.
When to use. Longest palindromic substring in O(n) (Manacher), shortest palindrome by prefix extension (KMP failure function), repeated/duplicate substrings (rolling hash, Z-algorithm).
Key idea. Manacher reuses palindrome symmetry to avoid recomputing; Z-algorithm computes longest common prefix with every suffix; suffix automaton/array enables substring queries.
Complexity. O(n) for Manacher and Z-algorithm; O(n log n) for suffix array.

📝 Sources & Notes

🌟 Universal Anchor Resources at the top of this page (NeetCode, Striver, AlgoMaster, GeeksforGeeks, CP-Algorithms, USACO Guide, VisuAlgo, USFCA, MIT OCW 6.006, CSES Handbook) cover ~90% of every pattern in the index. Start there.

Per-problem buttons:

  • 🎬 NC✓ (15 top problems) → research-verified direct NeetCode YouTube URL.
  • 📝 Sol → LeetCode community solutions tab.
  • 🎥 Video → YouTube search for "leetcode {problem} solution" — surfaces videos from all top channels (NeetCode, Striver/takeUforward, Code with Mike, Dinesh Varyani, AlgoZenith, etc.). No single channel forced, so you get whoever covered the problem best.
  • 📚 GFG → Google site:geeksforgeeks.org search — guaranteed working without 404s.

Subpattern fallback resources: Every subpattern has at least 2 resource links. Where a curated resource exists in the database, it's shown. Otherwise, an auto-generated Google site:geeksforgeeks.org search + YouTube tutorial search are inserted using the subpattern name — guaranteeing 100% subpattern coverage with zero broken links.

Progress tracking: Click the checkbox left of any problem to mark it solved. Progress is saved in your browser's localStorage (private to your device). The overall progress bar and per-pattern bars update live. Filter by Solved/Unsolved to focus your study.

Sort options: LC # (default), Name A→Z, Difficulty E→H, Difficulty H→E. Sort applies within each subpattern.

Sign-up wall caveats: The AlgoMaster blog uses a Substack soft email wall (content is readable). Medium/basecs is metered. Everything else listed is fully open with no login required.

Curated list membership: Blind 75 · NeetCode 150 · Grind 75.

Problem placements follow the source DOCX (16 patterns, 99 subpatterns from Thita.ai) with research additions (13 new patterns, 59 new subpatterns). All 88 cross-listed problems intentionally appear in multiple subpatterns because they exemplify more than one technique.

Note on UI: This page is inspired by takeUforward's Blind 75 detailed solutions page — sticky filter/sort bar, status checkboxes, per-pattern progress bars, theme toggle, print-friendly mode.
